items.title: What’s Happening to the WNBA Isn’t Normal
items.description: Let’s start with the good: The WNBA is more popular than ever. During the offseason, the league and the WNBA Players Association reached a landmark collective-bargaining agreement resulting in a 400 percent increase, on average, in player salaries . The average franchise valuation has soared 59 percent in the past year ; the Golden State Valkyries were appraised at a league-high $850 million. Between now and 2030, the WNBA will add three new teams, in Cleveland, Detroit, and Philadelphia. And the WNBA saw a 44 percent jump in ratings for this year’s All-Star Game—which, for the first time ever, hosted more in-person fans than the NBA’s . Yet this success has come amid unprecedented controversy. In early July, a group of 11 Republican lawmakers sent a letter to Cathy Engelbert, the WNBA’s commissioner, demanding that she be held accountable for not adequately addressing “repeated acts of unnecessary physical hostility and violence” on the court against the Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark, who has emerged as one of the league’s most popular players. The letter also suggested that these acts may be “racially motivated” against Clark, who is white, and called for the Department of Justice to investigate. And right before the All-Star Game, Clark’s teammate Sophie Cunningham told ESPN , “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” which immediately became a massive talking point around and outside the league. Shortly thereafter, multiple rallies sprang up in support of Cunningham; Celeste Keaton, a co-owner of the Seattle Storm, was suspended after verbally confronting a pair of teenage fans during a game who were holding signs supporting Cunningham. The discussions surrounding Cunningham and Clark have different origins; nonetheless, because they play together, their respective dramas have snowballed into one messy dispute that now envelops the league. Engelbert has certainly guided the league into its most financially stable era, but this is a complicated crossroads requiring delicate steering. Even if the WNBA isn’t in immediate danger of losing popularity, culture wars can be exhausting over time. And because its explosive success is the very thing attracting many of its critics, a narrative course correction may not be so simple. But the league needs to protect its players, and be careful not to kowtow too much to its critics. Managing the WNBA responsibly is especially challenging in this political and media environment. As Media Matters for America recently noted , Fox News has dedicated at least 206 segments to the WNBA since late June, most of which revolved around racial issues or the inclusion of trans athletes in the league. It’s difficult to refocus attention when a major news network isn’t letting up. Much of what’s happening now began when Clark entered the league, in 2024. In a short time, her tenure has helped the WNBA transform financially and receive more mainstream attention. But Clark’s stratospheric popularity has been complicated to manage. By keeping her views private, she’s become a blank slate for anyone’s cause. Though she has never publicly acknowledged her own political leanings, prominent conservatives have wielded Clark against her own league to advance MAGA’s racial grievances. And whenever a perception emerges that Clark is being treated unfairly by her peers, the backlash is outsize. In June, the Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas was suspended after hitting Clark in the throat during a game, one of the incidents prompting the letter from the Republican lawmakers. It was a bad play, but aggressive physical contact is an inevitable part of sports . Yet it was treated as an outlier: Thomas, who is Black, told reporters that after her play with Clark went viral, she received death threats and was called racial slurs . The heated environment can be seen as part of a larger outcry. The league is about 70 percent Black, and anywhere from 25 to 35 percent queer; historically, its players have embraced progressive issues. In 2016, the Minnesota Lynx wore T-shirts calling for justice and accountability following the police-related deaths of Philando Castile and Alton Sterling . A few years later, Senator Kelly Loeffler of Georgia, a Republican, wrote a letter to Engelbert criticizing the league’s support of the Black Lives Matter movement. In response, players backed Raphael Warnock, who eventually won the seat from Loeffler in the 2020 election. This history has made the WNBA low-hanging fruit for MAGA figures, whether politicians or commentators, who use it to score cheap points with their base. Critics lacking a serious investment in women’s basketball can conveniently swoop in to recite their spiel, and pay no attention to the sport itself. When the league was less popular, its players may have been freer to express their opinions without blowback. Perhaps that’s no longer possible. During All-Star weekend, I spoke with the Lynx’s rookie sensation, Olivia Miles, who talked about the difficulty of using the league as a platform for other issues, given the current attention. “Learning how to navigate that through sports is not an easy thing to do, because everyone is watching us at all times,” she said. “There’s so many things that are said and done and criticized.” The freedom to voice one’s politics goes both ways, and in Cunningham, conservative critics have a figure whose beliefs explicitly align with theirs on one particular topic. In the ESPN profile, she characterized her politics as “very much in the middle.” But her actions have drawn polarized attention. In Minneapolis, Cunningham took pictures with the former college swimmer Riley Gaines, who for years has advocated to keep transgender women out of women’s sports, and whose activism has been far more explicitly partisan. (Gaines has said the Biden administration “pushed radical gender ideology every chance it got,” and campaigned for President Trump.) “I think it’s people just practicing their rights of freedom of speech and doing what other fans have been doing since the WNBA has started,” Cunningham told reporters of the rallies held in her support. “And so props to them, props to everyone who is able to be competent and be bold and courageous enough to speak their truths.” Now coaches and players are being peppered with questions about where they stand—even though the league has never had a trans-woman player. (Layshia Clarendon, who was the first WNBA player to undergo top surgery , identified as nonbinary and trans. They retired in 2024.) Clark, too, has been criticized for not backing Cunningham’s stance. Some, like the Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, are choosing to do their own form of counterprotesting. Reeve wore a T-shirt during a recent game against the Fever that read Trans Kids Belong ; ahead of the game, she defended trans rights to the media . “I’ve chosen to listen to transgender families, and what I know is exclusion is not the answer,” she said. This is a snapshot of the current WNBA experience—unprecedented growth and great basketball at risk of being swallowed up by the same culture wars plaguing the broader political landscape. Nearly every day brings some new development conflating the conflicts. Last week, the former NBA players Royce White and Enes Kanter Freedom announced their intentions to identify as transgender in order to play in the WNBA . (It’s highly unlikely they’ll be allowed in the league.) During a game, Cunningham received a hard foul ; the other player, the Chicago Sky’s DiJonai Carrington, was ejected and subsequently posted “WHITE PRIVILEGE” to social media. The implication, presumably, was that Carrington, who is Black, was more heavily penalized because of the perception that Cunningham, and by extension her image and outspokenness, needs to be protected. With the overall success of the league at stake, being dragged into the political fray may be a steep price to pay for visibility. Still, the players don’t seem ready to shut up and dribble. “I think it’s really important that we don’t lose something that’s a foundational truth in our league, to the growth,” Jonquel Jones, who plays center for the New York Liberty, told me during All-Star weekend. “There’s enough space where we can grow as a league but still continue to have our integrity and continue to operate in a certain type of way. I feel like we’re losing that a little bit.” [ Read: A brief exchange that shows the enormous difference between Trump and Obama ] Competitive friction is one thing—but all of the WNBA’s players, regardless of who they are and what they believe, are now being publicly harassed. Before the All-Star Game, members of the players’ union executive and justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion committees met with league officials to express their concerns about the escalation in abuse. Yet the players are, in many ways, subject to political dynamics outside their control. “We’ve experienced a lot of great changes, but the perspective I have, it really weighs heavily on—and I want to say this in a way that isn’t taken the wrong way—this isn’t a problem that was created by the players,” WNBA Players Association President Nneka Ogwumike told me. “So looking to us to always fix it is not the only way.” The question now is how the league can cool the rhetoric used around it. Clark, for example, has criticized the racism and misogyny that her fame has brought upon the WNBA, but that has done little to slow it down. When she was asked about the pregame demonstrations supporting Cunningham after a recent game against Minnesota, she opted for a generic, noncommittal answer . “I think it’s for leagues and the governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions, but our focus is on basketball,” she said. Perhaps she shouldn’t have to be more forceful—but soon enough, she may not have a choice. Meanwhile, Cunningham has taken a different approach. Detractors call her “MAGA Barbie,” a nickname she’s disavowed, although, at the very least, she’s played just enough footsie with MAGA to enrich her own personal brand. Nevertheless, she seems to recognize that things have gotten out of control: “I’m going to let people just do the speaking for themselves, but for me, I want to get back to basketball,” she said in early August . But how exactly can the league pivot back to basketball, especially during a time when outrage is so easily stoked? Last Wednesday, a task force of WNBA-team presidents and general managers met to discuss trans-athlete inclusion, as well as the abuse that many of their players have received. In a statement released after the meeting, the league denounced the outside criticism as “bad-faith efforts” that were meant to “demean or marginalize others.” The meeting didn’t result in any new eligibility guidelines regarding trans players, and it showed that the league is on the defensive—which won’t cut it. The WNBA doesn’t get the luxury of being conveniently neutral the way other leagues do, not when its Black and queer players remain easy targets. Yet while all of this has been going on, excellent basketball is still happening. The league hasn’t imploded. Clark and Cunningham are able to play without causing riots. Nobody’s taken the bait regarding White and Freedom’s trollish provocations. Perhaps the best thing the WNBA can do is stay firm in its own identity, even if a few brushfires get started in the process. A more visible commissioner with consistent messaging certainly could help. But all of this stems from the players feeling the freedom to express themselves—and, in turn, feeling confident in their capacity to navigate any criticism. In a way, the fuss around Clark and Cunningham shows that giving in to the social-media comments section isn’t the answer. The league needs to be who it is, and take whatever comes with it.

items.title: From ‘Indispensable’ Ally to Target of Annihilation
items.description: W hen the United States was looking for a way to talk to Iran about a nuclear deal more than a decade ago, it turned to Oman, asking the country to do something it had quietly done for years: make an impossible conversation possible. Because Washington and Tehran had no diplomatic relations, the U.S. felt that the most promising back channel to get a conversation started led through Muscat. Iran was skeptical but willing to sit down with U.S. officials, provided there was some very particular diplomatic choreography. At Tehran’s request, Oman’s government found a room with multiple doors, so that American and Iranian officials would not be seen entering together. Omani officials took the head of the table, to create the impression that it was more than a bilateral conversation. That session laid the groundwork for what ultimately became the 2015 nuclear pact. “Without Oman, I’m not sure there would be an Iran nuclear deal,” Jake Sullivan, one of the top U.S. officials involved in those talks, told me. But today, that pact lies in ruins. President Trump tore it up, then went to war with Iran. Oman has watched its standing with Washington collapse too. Earlier this week, Trump threatened to “bomb the shit” out of the sultanate unless it did what America demanded—adding another longtime ally to the list of countries he has threatened to attack. Oman, located on the southeastern edge of the Arabian Peninsula, is often overshadowed by its wealthier, more conspicuous neighbors, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, and by its more tumultuous neighbor, Yemen . Yet for decades, Oman punched above its weight diplomatically by serving as one of Washington’s most useful interlocutors in the Middle East, in part because it has maintained relationships with governments that Washington often cannot or will not talk to. Trump has accused the sultanate of undermining his efforts to strike a deal with Iran and end the war, which began at the end of February and are now in a stalemate . The Strait of Hormuz, which is central to the conflict with Tehran, is also at the center of Washington’s dispute with Oman. The maritime corridor used to carry one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied-natural-gas supplies before the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran began and Tehran closed the strait to traffic through drone, small-boat, and mine attacks. Trump responded with a U.S. blockade, which remains in place even though the deadline for Washington and Tehran to reach an interim deal and set the stage for broader talks over Iran’s nuclear program expired earlier this week, showing no sign of a breakthrough. Oman and Iran border opposite sides of the strait; their respective territorial waters meet in the 21-mile-wide choke point. The two countries have been in talks in recent weeks to restore commercial ‌shipping, which has dwindled to a trickle. Both countries have floated the idea of a service fee for passage through the strait, but other Gulf nations have objected. Trump has wavered on the issue, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio has repeatedly said that the strait must return to being an open and free waterway. Trump has vowed to declare the strait a U.S. territory. He recently claimed that the strait was reopened and that mines and other hazards have been cleared. Shipping trackers continue to show a rate of passage dramatically below prewar levels. Omani officials insist that charging for passage is within the country’s legal rights. When asked on Monday in the Oval Office whether he was out of patience ​with Oman, Trump told ​reporters: “No, I don’t think ⁠they behaved very well, but we’d handle them very easily, just like we do other things.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has separately threatened Oman with sanctions if Muscat facilitates fees for ships passing through the strait. A U.S. official familiar with the deliberations told me that the administration views Oman’s handling of the negotiations as “dishonorable,” accusing Omani intermediaries of publicly portraying the two sides as nearing an agreement while privately conveying proposals to U.S. officials that the latter viewed as unacceptable. The official also accused Oman of delivering false statements to the press, which Omani officials deny. But this much is clear: The role that Oman used to play for Washington as a useful regional intermediary is over—at least as long as Trump remains in office. T he president’s anger presents an unusually awkward problem for Washington and for Muscat. Oman is not some distant neutral country that wandered into an American dispute. It has spent decades deliberately cultivating its relationship with Washington. “Oman has decided its strategic importance is to be nonaligned the way Switzerland is nonaligned,” Jon Alterman, the chair in global security and geostrategy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told me. “It’s a relatively small, relatively poor place, surrounded by giants, and Oman has decided it will make itself indispensable to everyone—not because it helps everybody, but because it’s a place that can keep a secret and allows people to meet quietly and resolve conflicts.” [ Read: Trump’s new strategy of nothing ] Modern diplomatic relations between the United States and Oman date to 1972, but their history goes back much further. In 1833, President Andrew Jackson’s administration signed a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with Oman, then an important maritime power, as Washington sought to expand commercial ties in the region and protect American merchants operating in the Indian Ocean. An American consulate operated in Muscat from 1880 to 1915. In 1980, after the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Oman became the first Persian Gulf state to officially grant the U.S. access to its military facilities. Oman doesn’t host a large, permanent American base like the Al Udeid Air Base, near Doha, the capital of Qatar. But Washington does have access to Omani military facilities and ports. In 2019, the two countries expanded that arrangement to include Duqm and Salalah, two key ports on the Arabian Sea, allowing American ships to operate and resupply outside the Gulf before entering the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has also spent decades pursuing a foreign policy designed to maintain relationships across the region’s fault lines. It has good relations with Iran, maintains a security partnership with the United States, and has kept channels open to the Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia in Yemen. It has also maintained contact with Israel. This is often described as Omani “neutrality,” though some of the sultanate’s regional neighbors believe that it favors Tehran. That has sometimes put Oman at odds with its fellow Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which view Iran as a major regional security threat. Oman declined to join the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen in 2015 and stayed out of the 2017 regional blockade of Qatar. Muscat also maintained channels to the Houthis, whom Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have long battled. One Saudi official I spoke with offered a skeptical assessment: “Oman’s definition of neutrality has been questionable.” Oman rejects the idea that its connections to Iran, including its economic relationship with and ties to the Houthis, amount to complicity. Instead, it casts its ties as a relationship of economic and regional importance. Oman serves as an economic lifeline and reexport hub for Iran, absorbing trade activity that previously passed through the UAE. (The UAE announced this week that it is stopping all trade and financial transactions with Tehran.) Iran, meanwhile, supplies Oman with agricultural products and heavy materials. A senior Omani diplomat I spoke with described neutrality as a practical necessity for a small state surrounded by larger powers. Oman, the official argued, gets criticized from all sides. “The Iranians will tell us, You’re being too soft on the West ,” the official told me, while Western governments accuse Oman of being too soft on Iran. “And the Houthis will tell us we’re being too nice to the Saudis, and the Saudis will tell us we’re being too nice to the Houthis. It just goes with the territory.” But Oman’s independence—its ability to talk to all sides, even if it irritates the others—is precisely what has made Muscat useful to successive American administrations. O man’s record as an intermediary is unusually long. The country has helped secure the release of American detainees held by Iran. It has also facilitated contacts involving Yemen. In early 2013, a small group of senior American officials quietly boarded a military plane bound for Oman. For years, John Kerry had been nurturing a diplomatic channel with Muscat, meeting secretly with Omani officials while he was chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in hope of opening back-channel talks with Iran. As President Obama’s secretary of state, he gave the green light to dispatch top foreign-policy officials to Muscat, including then–Deputy Secretary of State William Burns and Sullivan, who was serving as national security adviser to then–Vice President Biden. Those talks helped form the basis for the 2013 interim nuclear agreement and, eventually, the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. During the Biden administration, Muscat hosted the U.S. special envoy for Yemen, Tim Lenderking, and brokered his first direct contacts and message exchanges with Houthi representatives. Oman “wanted peace in Yemen, and they were willing to travel to Sanaa to meet with the Houthis and pass messages to Houthi leadership and exert their influence where they could to help us achieve a durable peace,” Lenderking, who is now a principal at the Washington-based law firm Squire Patton Boggs, told me. In 2025, the Trump administration again turned to Oman to host negotiations with Iran. Trump subsequently thanked Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, the country’s leader, for Oman’s role. [ Read: The art of the giveaway ] In addition to serving as an intermediary, Oman offers Washington military access and a stable partner near one of the world’s most important maritime choke points; Oman gets a powerful security partner while preserving the freedom to maintain its own relationships. But that bargain hinges on Oman’s independence. Analysts told me that this is why the current rupture matters. If the U.S. wants Oman to function as an intermediary, it cannot simultaneously demand that Muscat adopt Washington’s preferred position toward Iran. The very quality that makes Oman useful—the ability to talk to everyone—can look like disloyalty. That old paradox has now become a crisis. Oman says that it is trying to fulfill its obligations under international law and keep commercial shipping moving, including through Omani territorial waters. The Omani diplomat told me that the country’s lawyers believe that maritime fees can be lawful under international practice and that Oman has no intention of doing anything illegal. Trump and his negotiators see the issue differently, particularly where any arrangement could give Iran greater control over shipping or legitimize Iranian fees in what Tehran could portray as a victory over its much more powerful nemesis. Other nations have stepped in to play crucial mediating roles in this conflict, thus far to no avail. But Muscat remains one of the few doors available to American negotiators. The difficult question now is whether Trump’s threats will finally slam it shut.

items.title: Las mafias encarecen hasta los 9.000 euros lo que cobran a los migrantes por llevarles de Ceuta a la Península
items.description: Trayectos de horas en pequeñas embarcaciones, por la noche, hacinados y sin chalecos salvavidas ni medidas de seguridad. Un viaje penoso y peligroso, pero también muy caro para ir desde Ceuta hasta la Península. Las mafias de tráfico ilícito de migrantes han encontrado en la entrada masiva de miles de personas a nado en Ceuta del pasado 30 y 31 de julio un filón para incrementar su ya lucrativo negocio. Agentes de la Brigada de Extranjería de la Policía Nacional han detenido en los últimos días a cinco presuntos integrantes de dos grupos criminales que cobraban hasta 9.000 euros ―un precio superior al habitual, según fuentes cercanas a las pesquisas― a aquellas personas en situación irregular que quieren cruzar de modo clandestino el Estrecho de Gibraltar para llegar a las costas andaluzas, según ha informado este viernes el Ministerio del Interior. Las últimas estimaciones oficiales cifran en 5.000 migrantes ―aunque otras fuentes doblan este número― los que permanecen en Ceuta de los más de 80.000 que a finales de julio entraron a nado en la ciudad autónoma. De los que quedan, más de 2.000 son menores de edad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Budget 2026 : 410 milliards pour la Défense et la Sécurité
items.description: © Internet Plus du quart des dépenses exécutées par l’État au premier semestre 2026 a concerné la Défense et la Sécurité. Cette concentration intervient au moment où les recettes progressent plus rapidement que les décaissements, avant l’application complète d’un budget rectificatif qui accroît encore les besoins de financement. À la date du 30 juin, les dépenses du budget général atteignaient 1 507,502 milliards de francs CFA, soit 43,63 % des crédits prévus pour l’année, selon la situation d’exécution budgétaire publiée par le ministère de l’Économie et des Finances. Sur cette enveloppe, le ministère de la Défense et des Anciens combattants a exécuté environ 314 milliards de francs CFA. La Sécurité et la Protection civile ont mobilisé près de 95 milliards. Ensemble, ces deux départements représentent quelque 409 milliards de francs CFA, soit un peu plus de 27 % des dépenses effectuées pendant les six premiers mois. Rapporté à la période, l’effort équivaut à environ 2,26 milliards de francs CFA par jour. La comparaison donne aussi la mesure des choix budgétaires : l’Éducation nationale totalise près de 195 milliards de francs CFA et la Santé environ 151 milliards. Les crédits exécutés au titre de la Défense et de la Sécurité dépassent ainsi de plus de 60 milliards les dépenses cumulées de ces deux départements sociaux. Cette lecture par ministère demande toutefois une précaution. Elle ne couvre pas nécessairement l’ensemble des interventions publiques en faveur de l’éducation ou de la santé, dont certaines peuvent être portées par d’autres structures ou des comptes spécifiques. Elle montre néanmoins le poids central pris par la sécurité dans l’utilisation effective des ressources. Arbitrages Face à ces dépenses, les recettes du budget général ont atteint 1 814,240 milliards de francs CFA, correspondant à 61,82 % des prévisions. L’écart de 306,738 milliards observé avec les décaissements traduit surtout une différence de rythme à mi-année. Il ne constitue pas un excédent budgétaire annuel, compte tenu des dépenses restant à réaliser, des opérations de trésorerie et du déficit prévu sur l’ensemble de l’exercice. Les Impôts ont fourni environ 844 milliards de francs CFA et les Douanes 533,743 milliards au premier semestre. À fin juillet, les recettes douanières étaient passées à 632,314 milliards, soit près de 65 % de leur objectif annuel de 975 milliards. La performance la plus singulière vient des Domaines et du Cadastre. Avec 334,74 milliards de francs CFA recouvrés pour une prévision annuelle de 270 milliards, cette administration avait déjà dépassé son objectif d’environ 64,74 milliards. La composition de ces recettes et leur caractère reproductible seront déterminants pour apprécier la solidité de cette progression. Adoptée après la clôture du semestre, la loi de finances rectificative a porté les dépenses prévues de 3 578,217 à 3 993,319 milliards de francs CFA. Les recettes ont été relevées à 3 372,895 milliards, tandis que le déficit prévisionnel est passé de 520,425 à 620,425 milliards. Les 415,103 milliards de dépenses supplémentaires doivent notamment couvrir les opérations de sécurisation du territoire, une subvention exceptionnelle à la CMDT et de nouvelles charges liées aux fonds miniers. Le second semestre devra donc conjuguer accélération des programmes publics, maintien des recettes fiscales et financement d’un déficit accru de 100 milliards de francs CFA.

items.title: Saint-Louis : 31 nouveaux logements sociaux lancés à Ngallèle
items.description: La Société nationale des habitations à loyer modéré (SN HLM) a lancé la troisième phase de son programme de logements sociaux à Ngallèle, à Saint-Louis. Trente et une villas de type « Diariatou » et « Khadidja », bâties sur des parcelles de 200 m², sont prévues. Le programme vise à faciliter l’accès à la propriété pour les ménages sénégalais, y compris ceux de la diaspora. Après les deux premières phases, la SN HLM poursuit son programme de logements sociaux à Saint-Louis. Le directeur général de la société, Pape Abdourahmane Dabo, s’est rendu à Ngallèle pour lancer officiellement la troisième phase, en présence du gouverneur de Saint-Louis, Al Hassan Sall. Avant le lancement du nouveau chantier, les deux responsables ont visité les logements déjà réalisés. Le gouverneur s’est félicité de la qualité des constructions et des commodités proposées. « Nous avons constaté l’érection sur ce site de logements de qualité, de grandes villas bâties sur des surfaces assez intéressantes, avec toutes les commodités et des matériaux de qualité », a-t-il déclaré. Cette troisième phase prévoit la réalisation de 31 villas de type Diariatou et Khadidja. Les logements sont construits sur des parcelles de 200 m² et proposés à des prix annoncés entre 34 et 39 millions de francs CFA hors taxes. Leur acquisition est prévue sous le régime de la location-vente, avec des échéances pouvant s’étaler sur 15 à 25 ans. Pour Pape Abdourahmane Dabo, ce mécanisme doit permettre à des ménages disposant de revenus moyens d’accéder progressivement à la propriété. Le programme cible notamment les Sénégalais ayant un revenu mensuel d’au moins 400 000 francs CFA. « La vision, c’est un Sénégalais, un toit », a-t-il souligné, précisant que le dispositif est également ouvert aux Sénégalais de la diaspora. La réalisation du projet a été confiée à l’entreprise Delta, à l’issue d’un appel d’offres. Le directeur général de la SN HLM se dit confiant quant à la capacité de l’entreprise à respecter les délais prévus. Les travaux doivent s’achever dans un délai prévisionnel de huit mois. Le gouverneur Al Hassan Sall a, pour sa part, appelé à maintenir cette dynamique et à respecter les engagements pris. Il rappelle que l’accès au logement à des prix raisonnables constitue une orientation importante des politiques publiques. « L’objectif essentiel, c’est de les faire dans des délais records, dans un temps raisonnable », a-t-il insisté. Au-delà des chiffres et des délais, cette nouvelle phase porte l’espoir de nombreuses familles à la recherche d’un logement décent. À Ngallèle, les futures villas doivent ainsi contribuer à transformer progressivement le rêve d’un « toit » en réalité pour leurs futurs occupants. Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)

items.title: Les acteurs de la pêche invités à privilégier le marché local et la transformation des produits halieutiques
items.description: Les acteurs de la pêche doivent privilégier le marché local et s’investir davantage dans la transformation des produits halieutiques afin de renforcer la souveraineté alimentaire du Sénégal et de créer davantage de valeur ajoutée et d’emplois dans le secteur, a plaidé l’économiste Moustapha Dème. “Le secteur de la pêche est un géant. C’est un secteur qui produit en moyenne près de 500 000 tonnes de poissons, emploie des milliers de personnes, fait vivre une grande partie des Sénégalais et contribue aux exportations”, a-t-il déclaré. M. Dème s’exprimait en marge d’un dialogue sur la politique de la pêche entre le Sénégal et l’Union européenne, une rencontre organisée par la Fondation Konrad Adenauer, jeudi, à Mbour. Il a fait observer que le secteur de la pêche reste confronté à plusieurs défis, notamment la surpêche, la surcapacité de la flotte, le surinvestissement et la pêche illicite. “Aujourd’hui, il n’y a pas suffisamment de poissons pour les Sénégalais, malgré ce potentiel halieutique”, a-t-il déploré, estimant qu’une partie importante des ressources débarquées est destinée aux marchés extérieurs. L’économiste, également consultant, a particulièrement déploré l’exportation de produits halieutiques “en l’état”, notamment des petits pélagiques congelés entiers, qui sont ensuite transformés dans d’autres pays. “Les femmes transformatrices auraient pu accéder à cette matière, transformer ces produits et permettre au Sénégal d’exporter des produits élaborés, transformés, qui créent de la richesse nationale, de la valeur ajoutée et consolident les emplois”, a-t-il soutenu. Pour M. Dème, la question de l’accès des pêcheurs aux ressources ne relève pas seulement des moyens disponibles, mais relève surtout d’un “choix politique”. Il estime que l’État dispose de leviers permettant de maintenir davantage de produits halieutiques sur le marché national, notamment au profit des consommateurs et du secteur de la transformation artisanale. “Je ne suis pas contre les exportations, mais il faut que le Sénégal exporte des produits élaborés qui ont créé de la valeur ajoutée et qui ont consolidé les emplois au niveau de la transformation artisanale”, a-t-il insisté. Il a ainsi plaidé pour une réorientation de la politique d’exportation des produits de la pêche, en cohérence avec les objectifs de souveraineté alimentaire, afin de mieux valoriser les ressources halieutiques et de renforcer les chaînes nationales de transformation.

Special forces deployed in restive South Darfur capital Nyala
items.description: Special forces have been deployed in Nyala to maintain internal security, on the orders of the commander of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and head of the Security and Defence Council of the Sudan Founding Alliance ( Tasees ) government, Lt Gen Mohammed Hamdan ‘Hemedti’ Dagalo. Following the deployment of the special forces, security checks and surveillance operations intensified on the streets of Nyala. One of the commanders of the special forces deployed in Nyala said their mission, under decisions by the Security and Defence Council, was to protect citizens and their security, and to uphold the authority of the state in Nyala and other cities under the control of Tasis forces. The move follows a prolonged period of deteriorating security in Nyala, which has continued over the past two years. In a related development, urologist Dr Ammar Ahmed survived an assassination attempt in Nyala by a group travelling in vehicles belonging to the RSF, according to a statement issued by the Sudan Doctors Network on Thursday. Dr Ahmed was shot during the attack as he was leaving the hospital where he works. He was taken to another hospital in Nyala for treatment. The doctors’ network condemned the targeting of medical staff and health workers, and called for an end to violations and attacks against doctors and other healthcare workers. It also called for their safety and protection while carrying out their duties, particularly in conflict areas where medical services are most urgently needed. The network also called on local and international authorities to take urgent action to stop attacks on medical personnel and hold those responsible to account. Panthères du Gabon : Migné, trois ans pour écrire l’histoire
items.description: Nommé à la tête des Panthères du Gabon le 15 juillet dernier, Sébastien Migné a officiellement signé, le 20 août 2026, son contrat de trois ans avec la Fédération gabonaise de football. Le technicien français est désormais attendu sur deux fronts majeurs : qualifier le Gabon pour la CAN 2027 et tenter d’ouvrir, pour la première fois, les portes d’une phase finale de Coupe du monde. Le président de la Fégafoot, Pierre Alain Mounguengui et le nouveau sélectionneur des Panthères du Gabon, Sébastien Migné, le 20 août 2026. © D.R. Sébastien Migné prend les commandes d’une sélection qui ne manque ni de talent ni d’ambition, mais qui peine encore à transformer son potentiel en résultats dans les moments décisifs. Son contrat de trois ans, officialisé le 20 août avec la Fédération gabonaise de football (Fégafoot), fixe un cap clair : conduire les Panthères vers la CAN 2027 et, surtout, tenter de décrocher une qualification historique pour la Coupe du monde. Les dernières campagnes ont pourtant montré des signes encourageants. Le Gabon avait notamment validé son billet pour la CAN 2025, confirmant les capacités d’un groupe capable de rivaliser avec des adversaires de haut niveau. Mais certaines fragilités demeurent, notamment dans la gestion défensive, les périodes de baisse de régime et les fins de rencontres à forte pression. L’élimination face au Nigeria lors du barrage pour le Mondial en constitue une parfaite illustration. Accrochées jusqu’au terme du temps réglementaire, les Panthères ont finalement cédé durant la prolongation, s’inclinant lourdement (4-1). Un scénario qui met en évidence la nécessité de progresser dans la gestion physique, tactique et mentale des moments importants. Travailler sur la solidité collective Le nouveau staff devra ainsi travailler sur la solidité collective, la maîtrise des temps faibles et l’utilisation optimale des ressources disponibles sur le banc. Dans les matches à enjeu, ces détails peuvent faire basculer une rencontre et transformer une prestation prometteuse en qualification historique. Sébastien Migné mesure pleinement l’ampleur du défi. « J’ai trouvé que c’était une formidable opportunité d’essayer de créer quelque chose de nouveau, puisque le pays ne s’est encore jamais qualifié pour la Coupe du monde », a-t-il déclaré. Conscient des difficultés qui l’attendent, le technicien français se veut néanmoins ambitieux : « Ça ne sera pas évident, pas facile. Le chemin sera long, mais on va essayer de faire rêver toute une population et une fédération ». Pour concrétiser cette ambition, le sélectionneur devra également bénéficier d’un environnement stable, d’une préparation adaptée et de moyens à la hauteur des objectifs fixés. La Fégafoot et le ministère des Sports auront donc un rôle déterminant dans l’accompagnement du projet. Au-delà du changement de sélectionneur, le défi consiste désormais à bâtir une équipe capable de répondre présente dans les grands rendez-vous. Le Gabon dispose des joueurs, du talent et de l’ambition. À Sébastien Migné de transformer ces atouts en constance et en résultats. Le pari est lancé : écrire une nouvelle page de l’histoire du football gabonais. L’article Panthères du Gabon : Migné, trois ans pour écrire l’histoire est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Sudan’s women leaders: ‘El Burhan’s dialogue meaningless without a ceasefire’
items.description: Sudanese women political and human rights leaders have criticised army chief Abdelfattah El Burhan’s call for political dialogue , saying that any political process not preceded by clear steps to stop the war, create a suitable environment and ensure genuine participation by civilian forces risks becoming an attempt to reproduce past political experiences rather than address the roots of the crisis. Speaking to Radio Dabanga’s Radio Dabanga’s Kandakas & Miarems programme, they said a political process launched without these steps could ultimately fail to address Sudan’s crisis. ‘El Burhan seeking to make himself president’ Hiba Ahmed, a member of the leadership bureau of the opposition Beja Congress, told Radio Dabanga that the current call for political dialogue was intended, in her view, to prevent any genuine dialogue that could lead to an end to the war and address its root causes. She said army chief Abdelfattah El Burhan was seeking to consolidate his political position and install himself as president of the republic. Ahmed accused the Islamist movement of designing the current dialogue process in order to return fully to power and pursue its political and ideological agenda. She said talk of guarantees, amnesty and temporary immunity was not based on sound political or legal foundations, describing the proposals as an attempt to reassure political forces without providing genuine guarantees. She called for adherence to the plan announced by the Quad in September 2025, which, she said, links an end to the war with a political process. This should begin with a humanitarian truce leading towards a ceasefire, guarantees for the delivery of humanitarian aid and the protection of civilians, followed by a political process. Ahmed said her position was that the National Congress Party and the Islamist movement should not participate in the next political process. Any dialogue that did not clearly address these issues, she said, would not bring the crisis to an end. UNFPA Regional Director for Arab States, Leila Bakr, is pictured with a group of displaced women in a safe space in Port Sudan (File photo: UN News) Ceasefire first Sudanese lawyer, human rights activist, and international law expert Noon Kashkoush said al-Burhan’s statements on dialogue, guarantees and amnesty represented, in her view, a pattern repeated throughout Sudan’s political history, in which military and coup governments sought political legitimacy by launching dialogue initiatives. In an interview with Radio Dabanga, Kashkoush compared the current initiative with what became known during ousted president Omar Al Bashir’s rule as the “National Dialogue” or “El Wathba Dialogue”. She said the focus of such initiatives sometimes shifted towards the form and slogans of dialogue rather than its substance and the fundamental issues it was supposed to address. Any political dialogue taking place while the war continued, without addressing the issue of ending the fighting, would remain, in her view, “empty of substance”, she said. The priority should be negotiations with the parties to the conflict to reach a ceasefire and humanitarian truce before moving to the political stage. The political process, she said, should come later, with agreement on its structure and participants following an end to the war. She noted that many civilian forces were insisting that the National Congress Party be excluded from any future political process. She also criticised the use of laws to restrict the movement of political leaders and civilian activists, saying this undermined confidence in any guarantees offered in relation to dialogue or amnesty. The current environment, she said, did not provide sufficient guarantees for a serious political process. Kashkoush described the current call for dialogue as a “media stunt” and an attempt to seek political legitimacy. She warned that continued war and the absence of a genuine settlement could push Sudan towards an even more complicated reality, including entrenching divisions between areas controlled by different forces. UN Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher with a group of displaced women fleeing El Fasher in Tawila in November 2025 (File photo: UN) Declaration of principles before dialogue Azza Mohamed Ahmed, a member of the Women for Peace and Security group, said dialogue was not in principle unacceptable. It remained necessary and inevitable regardless of how long the war continued, she said, but stressed that it must not be used to serve the interests of a particular political party. The group includes women from conflict-affected areas of Darfur, South and West Kordofan, Blue Nile and eastern Sudan. Ahmed told Radio Dabanga that any serious dialogue should be preceded by extensive discussions on the fundamental issues, foremost among them ending the war and the guarantees needed to make any new truce successful, particularly given the reservations of the parties to the conflict about the outcome of previous truces. She called for an official and clear declaration of principles before dialogue begins, setting out the issues to be discussed and the objectives being pursued. It should also address questions over whether the fighting can be stopped, the terms of any truce and the guarantees required to implement it. Such a declaration, she said, was a necessary first step towards creating the conditions for any serious political process. items.title: Cameroun : résultats du GCE annoncés à deux semaines de la rentrée scolaire
items.description: © DR Les candidats ayant composé les épreuves des examens General Certificate of Education ne sont pas fixés sur leur sort alors que la communauté éducative prépare la rentrée pour le compte de la prochaine année scolaire. La délivrance est tout de même annoncée. Sept semaines après la fin des épreuves reportées du GCE, les oreilles sont tournées vers le GCE Board dans l'attente des résultats des examens. Les candidats et leurs parents, se posent encore la question : « Près de deux mois déjà, mais à quand les résultats ? ». À la moindre rumeur sur la publication de ces derniers, les cœurs battent la chamade. Et les le vide favorise la prolifération des fausses nouvelles. Des communiqués issus des sources aux intentions sans doute malveillantes, inondent la toile. Certains prétendent que les examens sont annulés. D'autres annonçant que les résultats sont disponibles. La réalité est pourtant tout autre. À la différence des sessions antérieures, les résultats de la session 2026 arrivent avec un léger retard comme en 2022 où ils étaient rendus publics le 19 août peu avant à la rentrée scolaire. Les deux sessions suivantes, les candidats étaient fixés sur leur sort le 24 juillet 2023 et la même date en 2024. En 2025, c'est le 1er août que le GCE Board a livré la copie des examens. Cependant, à chaque session, un contexte particulier. Celui de 2026 est la fraude massive ayant entaché le déroulement des épreuves écrites. Prévues pour passer entre le 08 juin et le 18 juillet 2026, certaines épreuves ont été reportées entre le 22 juin et le 02 juillet 2026. La suspension de la session et la reprise en raison de la fuite massive des épreuves sur les réseaux sociaux serait l'origine principale du retard de la publication des résultats. Néanmoins, dans les coulisses, des sources bien introduites dans la gouvernance de l'institution chargée de l'organisation des examens GCE annoncent l'imminence de la publication des résultats de la session 2026. Pour certains, ce n'est plus qu'une affaire d'heures. Pour d'autres, il n'y a pas de certitude. Dans tous les cas, l'attente se poursuit, même si le bout du tunnel s'annonce. Comme annoncé plus haut, voici les résultats du GCE A and O Level session 2026 publiés quelques heures après cet article. Cet article Cameroun : résultats du GCE annoncés à deux semaines de la rentrée scolaire est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: CNSS–CPPF : un pas de plus vers la continuité des droits à la retraite
items.description: La Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS) et la Caisse des pensions et des prestations familiales des agents de l’État (CPPF) ont achevé, le 19 août 2026, les travaux préparatoires visant à mettre en place un mécanisme de coordination des régimes de pensions de vieillesse des secteurs public et privé. Une avancée destinée à mieux protéger les travailleurs ayant effectué une partie de leur carrière dans chacun des deux secteurs. Les responsables de la CNSS et de la CPPF lors des échanges, le 19 août 2026. © CNSS Réunis au sein du Comité de validation, les représentants de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS) et la Caisse des pensions et des prestations familiales des agents de l’État (CPPF) ont procédé à l’examen des travaux menés par la Commission paritaire chargée de définir les mécanismes techniques et juridiques nécessaires à cette coordination. L’objectif est notamment de mieux prendre en compte les carrières professionnelles mixtes, devenues de plus en plus fréquentes avec la mobilité des travailleurs entre les secteurs public et privé. Photo de famille à l’issue des travaux. © CNSS Au cœur des discussions figure le principe de totalisation des périodes d’activité accomplies auprès des deux régimes. Il s’agit de permettre que les années de cotisation effectuées successivement ou alternativement dans le public et le privé puissent être prises en compte dans l’appréciation des droits à pension. Chaque organisme resterait toutefois chargé d’appliquer les dispositions prévues par sa propre législation. « L’objectif est de préserver les droits à pension des assurés ayant connu une carrière mixte entre les secteurs public et privé », ressort de cette démarche engagée conjointement par les deux caisses. Les travaux ont été conduits sur la base de la décision n°000006/26/CNSS-CPPF du 23 avril 2026 portant création et organisation de la Commission paritaire. Ils ont notamment permis de produire un projet de texte, une note de présentation, un rapport technique ainsi qu’un projet de rapport des travaux. Avec l’achèvement de cette phase technique, la CNSS et la CPPF considèrent avoir rempli la mission préparatoire qui leur avait été confiée. «Le relais est désormais transmis au gouvernement », à qui revient la responsabilité de donner les suites institutionnelles et réglementaires nécessaires à la mise en œuvre du mécanisme proposé. Cette étape constitue ainsi une avancée dans la recherche d’une meilleure articulation entre les régimes de pensions de vieillesse. Elle pourrait, à terme, contribuer à renforcer la continuité des droits sociaux des travailleurs dont les parcours professionnels alternent entre administration publique et secteur privé. La phase préparatoire étant désormais achevée, le processus entre donc dans une nouvelle séquence, désormais placée entre les mains des autorités gouvernementales compétentes.
